summary: Specifies a small modification to the ARP mechanism, without changing the packet format, that lets a node announce it is leaving the network so other nodes can update their ARP tables. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: UNARP lets a server announce that an IP-address mapping is no longer valid. Other computers that receive the announcement remove that entry from their ARP caches.

questions: how to remove an arp entry when a node leaves
how to remove an arp cache entry
how does unarp remove an arp entry
what does a proxy arp server do
subtitle: A broadcast that tells nearby nodes to remove an obsolete ARP mapping.

tldr.problem: A proxy ARP server can disconnect from a dial-in host while other computers still cache the server's hardware address for that host.
tldr.mechanism: The disconnecting server broadcasts an unsolicited ARP Reply called UNARP. A receiver deletes the cached mapping for the named IP address.
tldr.outcome: The Experimental proposal changes how nodes use ARP, not the ARP packet format; it sets the hardware-address length to zero so unsupported nodes should reject the abbreviated packet.

today: RFC 1868 is an Experimental protocol. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Why ARP Entries Become Stale
sections.content:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps a network address to a hardware address on a broadcast network. ARP does not require nodes to announce their presence periodically, so implementations commonly rely on timers to remove old entries.

Proxy ARP creates a case where a stale entry matters: a communication server can answer an ARP request for a remote dial-in host using its own hardware address. If that host reconnects through another server before the entry expires, traffic may still go to the first server.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP caches remember which hardware address reaches an IP address. A dial-in host can move to another server before the old cached route expires.

sections.title: The UNARP Announcement
sections.content:
When a server disconnects from a remote host for which it answered a Proxy ARP request, it broadcasts an unsolicited ARP Reply. The packet names the departing host's IP address as its source protocol address and uses 255.255.255.255 as its target protocol address.

The UNARP packet uses opcode 2, protocol address space 0x800, protocol address length 4, and hardware address length 0. It is 16 bytes, excluding the MAC header. A receiver deletes its ARP cache entry for the named IP address. A gracefully detaching host may send one for itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The server broadcasts an ARP Reply with the departing host's IP address. Computers that understand UNARP then delete their cached mapping for that address.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
UNARP leaves the ARP packet format unchanged but omits the source and target hardware-address fields by setting their length to zero. The RFC expects nodes that do not support UNARP to reject the packet rather than store a zero hardware address.

The RFC recommends a configuration switch to disable UNARP if a vendor's ARP implementation objects to the abbreviated packet. Its security section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet has no hardware-address values, which should make older nodes reject it. The RFC recommends a setting to turn UNARP off if a system cannot handle it.

references.text: Plummer, D., "An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol", STD 37, RFC 826, MIT, November 1982.
